title: Product quantization I: the compression idea
summary: Splitting a vector into m pieces and quantizing each independently gives 256^m representable vectors from m bytes. Measured, PQ alone at 64x compression gets recall 0.646, but used as a shortlist with a full-vector rescoring pass it gets 0.992, which is why it is a filter rather than a replacement.
html:
IVF changed which vectors you look at. It did nothing about how big they are. A billion 384-dimension float32 vectors is 1.5 TB whether you organise them or not, and that number is the reason this technique exists.

The obvious approach, and why it fails

You already know how to compress vectors: cluster them and store the centroid id. That is vector quantization, and it is what IVF's coarse quantizer does.

The problem is resolution. With k centroids you can represent exactly k distinct vectors. To approximate a million vectors usefully you would need hundreds of thousands of centroids, and now the codebook alone is as big as the data you were compressing. One byte per vector buys you 256 possible values for the whole vector. Useless.

The trick

Stop quantizing the whole vector. Cut it into m pieces and quantize each piece independently, with its own codebook.

384-dim vector, m = 24 subquantizers

[------ 384 floats ------]
 |  |  |  |  ...  |  |  |     24 subvectors of 16 dims each
 v  v  v  v       v  v  v
 7 203 19 88 ... 44 161 2     one centroid id per subvector = 24 bytes

Now count what you can represent. Each subvector has 256 choices, and the choices are independent, so the vector as a whole has 256^m possibilities:

m =  1 byte   ->  256^1  = 10^2   distinct vectors
m =  4 bytes  ->  256^4  = 10^10
m =  8 bytes  ->  256^8  = 10^19
m = 24 bytes  ->  256^24 = 10^58

Twenty four bytes addresses more distinct vectors than there are atoms in the observable universe. That combinatorial explosion is the "product" in product quantization: the representable set is the Cartesian product of the per-subspace codebooks.

Training is just k-means m times, once per slice of the dimensions. The codebooks are shared across the whole corpus, so they cost a fixed 1.5 MB or so regardless of whether you have a thousand vectors or a billion.

Why 256, and why this works at all

The k=256 you see everywhere is not tuned, it is the largest codebook that fits in one byte. Going to 65,536 would double the storage per subquantizer and need far more training data to fit the extra centroids, and dropping to 16 means bit-packing for a saving you can get more cleanly by raising m. One byte per subquantizer is the convenient point and almost everyone sits there.

The deeper question is why quantizing 16 dimensions with only 256 points works at all. In 16 genuinely independent dimensions it would not: 256 centroids spread over a 16-dimensional cube is hopeless coverage. It works because learned embedding dimensions are heavily correlated. The vectors do not fill their space, they lie near a much lower-dimensional surface inside it, so each subspace has far less going on than its dimension count suggests. PQ is exploiting the same redundancy that makes the embeddings compressible in the first place.

What it costs, measured

On the same 6,200 document embeddings, 384 dimensions, 1,536 bytes each uncompressed:

  m  dims/sub  bytes/vec  compress  cos(orig,recon)  recall@10
  6        64          6      256x           0.6155      0.420
 12        32         12      128x           0.6638      0.514
 24        16         24       64x           0.7523      0.646
 48         8         48       32x           0.8682      0.769
 96         4         96       16x           0.9623      0.874
192         2        192        8x           0.9971      0.965

Read that and PQ looks like a bad deal. 64x compression for a recall of 0.646 is not something you would ship.

That is because the table measures PQ doing a job it is not meant to do.

PQ is a filter, not a replacement

Nobody runs PQ as their final answer. The codes narrow millions of candidates down to hundreds, and then you score those hundreds against the full vectors. Same measurement, with a rescoring pass added:

  m  compress   PQ only   rescore top50   top100   top200
  6      256x     0.420           0.801    0.903    0.961
 12      128x     0.514           0.876    0.949    0.987
 24       64x     0.646           0.969    0.992    0.997
 48       32x     0.769           0.993    0.999    0.999

24 bytes per vector and recall@10 of 0.992, against 1,536 bytes uncompressed. The rescoring pass costs 100 full-precision dot products per query, which is nothing next to the millions you avoided.

Even the absurd setting works: 6 bytes per vector, a 256x reduction, gets 0.961 once you rescore 200 candidates. The lossy stage only has to get the right answer somewhere into a shortlist. Precision is the second stage's job.

This should feel familiar. It is a bloom filter in front of an expensive lookup, or a zone map that lets you skip blocks before reading them. Cheap approximate structure in memory, exact data behind it, and the approximation only needs to be good enough not to discard what you were looking for.

What this implies about where your data lives

Rescoring needs the full vectors, which means they have to be somewhere. That is the architecture rather than a footnote:

  • PQ codes in RAM. At 24 bytes, a billion vectors is 24 GB. That fits on one machine.
  • Full vectors on SSD. 1.5 TB, read only for the few hundred candidates per query.

You have inverted the memory problem. The thing you scan constantly is small enough to be resident, and the thing that is enormous is touched a few hundred times per query, which is exactly the access pattern Day 20 said storage is good at. Day 23 combines this with IVF, and Day 25 is what happens when a graph index adopts the same split.

Two honest caveats

My numbers are optimistic about training. With 256 centroids per subspace and 6,200 vectors, each centroid is fitted from about 24 points, which is thin. The usual guidance is at least a hundred points per centroid, so 25,000 vectors minimum before PQ behaves properly, and more is better. If you try this on a small corpus and the reconstruction looks bad, that is probably why rather than anything wrong with the method.

Second, the splitting is naive. I cut the 384 dimensions into contiguous blocks of 16, which assumes neighbouring dimensions belong together. In a learned embedding they do not, and some subspaces end up carrying far more variance than others, which wastes codebook capacity. Day 24 fixes this with a learned rotation.

One thing is still clumsy. To compare a query against a PQ code I reconstructed the approximate vector and took a dot product, which is a decode on every candidate. Tomorrow removes that entirely: asymmetric distance computation, where you precompute a small table once per query and then score candidates with table lookups and adds.
exercise:
1. Compute your own compression table. For your embedding dimension, work out bytes per vector at m = d/64, d/16 and d/4, and the resulting index size for your real corpus count. Put it next to the uncompressed figure from Day 9. One of those rows is the difference between needing a cluster and needing a laptop.

2. Implement encode and decode. Thirty lines: k-means per subspace to get codebooks, then argmin over each subspace to encode, then a lookup to reconstruct. Measure the cosine between original and reconstructed vectors at a couple of values of m. Watching a vector survive being crushed to 24 bytes is the point.

3. Prove the rescoring pattern. Using your codes, retrieve the top 100 by approximate distance, then re-rank those 100 with the full vectors and measure recall@10. Compare against recall@10 from the codes alone. The gap between those two numbers is why nobody ships PQ without a rescoring stage.
